A.name: Two-Tier (Client-Server)
A.summary: Direct client to MySQL database connection.

pros: Direct TCP socket yields minimal round-trip latency (Median 0.21 ms vs 4.59 ms in Mode B).
Zero intermediate serialization overhead (binary MySQL protocol; no JSON encoding/decoding).
Simpler architecture with fewer moving parts to maintain or deploy.
cons: Database credentials (client_user) must be distributed to end-user client devices.
Direct MySQL port (:3306) is exposed across network boundaries, increasing attack surface.
No centralized business logic layer: queries, validation, and transactions run client-side.
Schema changes require updating and redeploying every desktop client executable.

real_world_examples: LAN Accounting Software (e.g., Tally ERP multi-user client connecting to central data server)
Hospital & Clinic Desktop POS/Billing workstations accessing a central Microsoft SQL or MySQL server
University laboratory terminals running direct SQL client tools against a campus database server
Bloomberg Professional Terminal & SAP GUI thick enterprise workstations

B.name: Three-Tier (Web-App-DB)
B.summary: Segmented perimeter: Client -> Nginx TLS -> FastAPI -> MySQL.
B.firewall_rule: Client reaches :443 only. Web reaches :5000 only. App reaches :3306 only. Client->DB is default DROP.

pros: Defense-in-depth: Database server (10.0.3.10) is completely isolated on an internal subnet.
TLS termination at Web tier encrypts all public transit data; private queries stay internal.
Centralized business logic & validation: database schema and admin credentials never leak to clients.
Scalability: Web and Application tiers can be scaled horizontally behind load balancers.
cons: Higher operational latency due to multiple network hops, TLS negotiation, and JSON serialization overhead.
More containers, routing configs, and reverse proxy layers to monitor and secure.
Increased architectural resource footprint (Nginx + FastAPI + MySQL vs MySQL alone).

real_world_examples: Modern E-Commerce Platforms (Shopify, Amazon web client -> API gateway -> microservices -> DB)
Online Banking & Fintech Portals (customer browser -> TLS reverse proxy -> core banking API -> DB)
SaaS Web Applications (multi-tenant web frontends with strict backend data isolation)

provenance.environment: Docker Compose v2 / Linux kernel namespaces (internal: true subnets)

connection_reuse_persistent.description: Persistent connection reuse: Mode A reused MySQL socket vs Mode B reused HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive session.

per_request_connection.description: Per-request connection establishment: Mode A new TCP socket + MySQL handshake per query vs Mode B new TCP + TLS 1.3 handshake per request.

latency.limitations_note: Benchmark Limitations & Methodology Note: All measurements were executed on isolated bridge networks within a single host environment. While reflecting genuine kernel iptables packet routing, socket handling, and TLS/JSON serialization costs, they do not introduce multi-hop WAN propagation delays (10-100 ms). Database payload was fixed to 5 product records; network protocol overhead dominated over DB disk I/O. Concurrency was serialized (concurrency = 1); results do not capture MySQL connection pool contention or connection limits under high client concurrency in Two-Tier mode.

tls_comparison:
======================================================================
  MODE A (TWO-TIER) TRANSPORT SECURITY DEMONSTRATION
  Demonstrating that plaintext on port 3306 is a configuration choice
======================================================================

--- [1] Mode A with TLS Disabled (Plaintext) ---
  Transport Cipher : NONE (Plaintext Wire Traffic)
  TLS Version      : NONE
  Sample Query     : SELECT ... -> SKU-1001 ($99.99)

--- [2] Mode A with TLS Required (Encrypted) ---
  Transport Cipher : TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  TLS Version      : TLSv1.3
  Sample Query     : SELECT ... -> SKU-1001 ($99.99)

======================================================================
SUMMARY:
  Plaintext Mode : Cipher=NONE, TLS=NONE
  TLS Mode       : Cipher=TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS=TLSv1.3
  Conclusion: Two-Tier networks can enforce full TLS encryption on the wire.
======================================================================

===========================================================================
        BUSINESS LOGIC INTEGRITY & PRICE TAMPERING DEMONSTRATION
        Comparing Two-Tier (Mode A) vs Three-Tier (Mode B)
===========================================================================

===========================================================================
        BUSINESS LOGIC INTEGRITY & PRICE TAMPERING DEMONSTRATION
        Comparing Two-Tier (Mode A) vs Three-Tier (Mode B)
===========================================================================

===========================================================================
  [DEMO 1] MODE A (TWO-TIER): DIRECT CLIENT SQL INJECTION / PRICE TAMPER
===========================================================================
Scenario: A manipulated Mode A desktop client connects using client_user.
Goal: Purchase 'SKU-1002' (Catalog: $499.50) for $0.01.

[*] Target Product  : Dell UltraSharp 27 4K Monitor (SKU: SKU-1002)
[*] Real Catalog Price : $499.50
[*] Stock Before Sale : 15

[>] Client executing raw INSERT with manipulated unit_price = $0.01...
[!] SUCCESS (DATA INTEGRITY VIOLATED): Database accepted manipulated price!
    Invoice Created: INV-TAMPER-A-602003
    Billed Amount  : $0.01 (Expected: $499.50)
    Stock Decrement: 15 -> 14
    Underlying Grant: client_user has 'GRANT UPDATE (stock) ON shopledger.products'
                      and 'GRANT INSERT ON shopledger.invoice_items'.
    Key Takeaway    : The database verified SQL privileges, but had NO WAY
                      to verify application-level business rules!

===========================================================================
SUMMARY OF ARCHITECTURAL SECURITY TRADE-OFF:
  Mode A (Two-Tier)   : Tampered price accepted by DB because SQL grants
                        lack domain business logic context.
  Mode B (Three-Tier) : Tampered price actively detected and rejected with
                        HTTP 400 Bad Request by the application tier.
===========================================================================

        BUSINESS LOGIC INTEGRITY & PRICE TAMPERING DEMONSTRATION
        Comparing Two-Tier (Mode A) vs Three-Tier (Mode B)
===========================================================================

===========================================================================
  [DEMO 2] MODE B (THREE-TIER): MIDDLEWARE VALIDATION / TAMPER REJECTION
===========================================================================
Scenario: An attacker sends an HTTP request to FastAPI with a manipulated price.
Goal: Attempt to purchase 'SKU-1002' for $0.01 via the API.

[>] Sending HTTP POST with payload: {"customer_id": 1, "items": [{"product_sku": "SKU-1002", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": 0.01}]}...
[+] HTTP 400 Bad Request (SECURITY INVARIANT ENFORCED):
    API Server Response: {"detail":"Price manipulation rejected: Client submitted unit_price $0.01 does not match catalog price $499.50 for SKU 'SKU-1002'."}
    Key Takeaway       : In Three-Tier, the client NEVER talks to the database.
                         The FastAPI tier validates prices against the server catalog
                         and rejected the fraudulent price before it ever reached MySQL.

===========================================================================
SUMMARY OF ARCHITECTURAL SECURITY TRADE-OFF:
  Mode A (Two-Tier)   : Tampered price accepted by DB because SQL grants
                        lack domain business logic context.
